summary.title: An Archaeology-Inspired Database
summary.one_liner: Learn how to build an append-only, "functional" database in Clojure where updates add layers instead of overwriting data, so full history stays queryable.
keywords: how to keep old data in a database
takeaways: Updates, additions and removals are modeled as new layers on top of old data, so earlier states can be revealed again.
Facts are stored as datoms (entity-id, attribute-name, attribute-value) and organized in four indexes: EAVT, AVET, VEAT and VAET.
Clojure features such as immutable collections, atoms, protocols, records and metadata are used to build the in-memory store.
An evolution-of function walks the prev-ts chain to show how an attribute's value changed over time.
summary.summary: The chapter argues that conventional databases overwrite data in place, which loses history, and proposes an archaeology-inspired alternative where data is buried in layers rather than deleted. It then builds this "functional database" in Clojure step by step: records for databases, layers, entities and attributes, a storage protocol with an in-memory implementation, and four permutation indexes over datoms. Lifecycle operations (add, remove, update) are implemented by appending new layers, with reference cleanup handled through the VAET index. The code is shown inline with explanations of Clojure idioms such as destructuring, metadata and design-by-contract preconditions.
